programme.title: Primates – The Secret to Survival | E01
programme.desc: A documentary series devoted to our favorite primates, presenting species that are rarely shown on screen. Modern technology has enabled creators to capture their world from a unique perspective and in their natural environment, whether it is the treetops of a flood forest or the dense bushes shrouded in the darkness of a Sri Lankan night. Over the course of two years, the filmmakers undertook twenty-eight expeditions around the world, braving snowstorms in the Moroccan Atlas Mountains and wading through flooded jungles in remote corners of Sumatra and Brazil. They were among the first in history to immortalize the newly discovered Tapanuli orangutan species and were the first in years to attempt to film a white uakari. One team spent over two months in Equatorial Guinea, camping on a remote beach to record the most intimate scenes from the life of a mandrill, one of the least understood primates in the world. In Sri Lanka, thanks to low-light technology, the first color images of mysterious gray loris in the wild were captured at night. Captivating animal stories combine real family drama with cutting-edge science. A seemingly terrifying silver-backed mountain gorilla encountered on the volcanic slopes of the Congo turns out to be a gentle and caring father to its young. According to the latest research, it is caring fathers who achieve the greatest reproductive success. Viewers will also see South Africa's elusive pygmy galago, part of a recently discovered urban population, as it raids the local zoo at night. In Malaysia, they will learn about the world of treetops from the perspective of white-handed gibbons, shown on screen for the first time in history. The unique series is narrated by naturalist Chris Packham. Among the fog-covered slopes of volcanoes in the Congo Basin live some of the largest and most famous primates. Among them is a silver-backed mountain gorilla that uses a surprising strategy. He bases his domination and power on a bold show of force, thanks to which he maintains order in the family's life. However, when the offspring refuses to respect the father's authority, the dangerous tyrant reveals his gentler side. It turns out that this dangerous leader is more than just an aggressive guardian of the hearth. He can also be gentle and sensitive. Recent research shows that an alpha male must demonstrate more than just strength to be successful. Meanwhile, hard times have come for the herd of bearded capuchin monkeys living in the Brazilian highlands. The sun-baked canyons there haven't seen a drop of rain in eight months. However, monkeys have found a solution to the lack of food and water - they catch lizards, which are a source of protein and water, and also eat wild cashew nuts, which are rich in fats and minerals. In South Africa, nocturnal galagos are also searching for missing food. In Pretoria, under the cover of darkness, they raid the city zoo. While the park's predatory inhabitants sit in cages, the galagos can roam around without fear. Clever animals have learned to navigate zoos with an unusual trick to help them do so - they smear sticky drops of urine on their hands and feet to leave a trail of scent behind them and at the same time give their limbs extra traction for jumping. In India's Western Ghats, lion macaques have abandoned cooperation in favor of a strategy based on the exploitation of other animals. Giant squirrels have an excellent sense of smell adapted to recognize ripe jackfruit, so clever macaques allow them to use it to then steal the prey from the squirrels. Lemurs living in Madagascar constitute one fifth of all primates. This island is also the only place in the world where they can be found. Like many primates, lemurs are attacked by ticks and other parasites. However, we meet a group of blue-eyed lemurs that have developed a brilliant way of dealing with pests - self-medication. USA, Great Britain. 2020. documentary film

Using stunning outdoor photography from around the world and interviews with experts, they chronicle the rise of prehistoric megabeasts, from woolly mammoths to saber-toothed cats. They also present the history of the fight between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens. They will discover the secrets of the era that created the world we live in. It turns out that another extreme temperature drop on Earth may be caused by... climate change and global warming. Steve Backshall and Michaela Strachan explore the history of the woolly mammoth and the saber-toothed cat. Thanks to modern technologies, these huge mammals are brought back to life. Researchers are looking for answers to the question of why animals perfectly adapted to extreme conditions became extinct when the ice began to melt. Michaela discovers a weakness of a prehistoric hunter that may have contributed to his extinction. Meanwhile, Steve learns about a revolutionary gene-editing technique that can revive mammoths. Great Britain. 2022. documentary film

programme.title: Ice Age: Frozen World | E02
programme.desc: Naturalist and explorer Steve Backshall and wildlife presenter Michaela Strachan take viewers on a gripping journey into the heart of the Ice Age. Using stunning outdoor photography from around the world and interviews with experts, they chronicle the rise of prehistoric megabeasts, from woolly mammoths to saber-toothed cats. They also present the history of the fight between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens. They will discover the secrets of the era that created the world we live in. It turns out that another extreme temperature drop on Earth may be caused by... climate change and global warming. The Ice Age became an arena of struggle between Neanderthals and representatives of Homo sapiens. Steve Backshall and Michaela Strachan investigate how two competing species have adapted to extreme conditions. Backshall explores southern Germany, where he discovers traces of the life of early humans and their ability to deal with prehistoric predators using advanced tools and weapons. In turn, Strachan examines the differences in anatomy and skills between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens. It turns out that despite the physical advantage of the former, the latter showed greater abilities in long-distance running and technological innovation. The key technology that gave them the advantage was the sewing needle, which allowed them to create tighter clothing. The decisive moment that led to the extinction of Neanderthals was global warming and environmental changes that left Homo sapiens as the dominant species. Great Britain. 2022. documentary film
